cells.tense: You're standing in the clearing with your hands already on what comes next, and you know it's yours to tend.
cells.ask: let one finished thing be done, and let the finishing be enough — that's how the ground gets ready for what you plant next.
cells.core:
The false structure came down and you didn't rush to rebuild it. That's what tending looks like when it's going well here: you can hold two needs in the same hand without dropping either, you can decide what to keep and what to cut back, and the deciding doesn't tear at you. The care is steady. People and projects come to you because they can tell you'll carry them without crushing them. That steadiness is what makes the cleared ground safe for whatever grows next.

There's a thing that's finished, and some part of you is still holding it open. Let it close. Release what's done and feel what that frees. A thing ending isn't a loss. It's the ground being ready.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending the open ground with steady hands, and you're not forcing it.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, responsible care — deciding what to keep, what to cut back, and what to hand on
cells.place: in the sudden clearing, after a structure that couldn't hold has come down and left open ground

cells.tense: You're already three plantings ahead of the clearing, bracing for a harvest that hasn't been seeded yet.
cells.ask: let one future you're clutching stay unimagined for a day — a dream that has room to breathe is one you can actually live in.
cells.core:
When this is going well, the clearing is a place of real possibility — you can see what could grow here and the seeing is generous, unhurried, grounded in what's actually in your hands. You imagine from what you've already lived, so the dream lands. Care doesn't exhaust you because you're not carrying more than is yours.

Right now you're ahead of the ground. Every two demands get gripped so hard that neither roots, and the future you're protecting hasn't been seeded yet. The care that should be steady has gone tense. You're tending a harvest that isn't yours to tend today. Set it down. What's worth building will still be worth building when you come back — and it'll come back bigger if you let it rest.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding the next season so hard the current one can't grow.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, responsible care — deciding what to keep, what to cut back, and what to hand on

cells.tense: The clearing opened behind you, and you're still standing at the edge of it, not stepping in.
cells.ask: plant one small thing in the open ground this week, however badly — doing it at all is the way back to being someone who tends.
cells.core:
In its healthy form this is unhurried care that keeps its hands in the dirt — you know what belongs to you, you tend it at its own pace, and the growth that comes is quiet and real. Tending like that doesn't exhaust you because you're not clutching; you're holding space and letting things be what they are.

The false structure came down and you stepped back from what it left. There's open ground and you're not in it — not because you chose to leave, but because the collapse took the tending with it. The care didn't disappear. The doing stopped.

One small thing, planted this week. Not a plan, not a project — something you can touch and watch. Doing it badly counts.
cells.sheetLine: The ground is cleared and waiting, and you haven't stepped in.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, responsible care — deciding what to keep, what to cut back, and what to hand on
cells.place: in the sudden clearing, after a structure that couldn't hold has come down and left open ground

cells.tense: You're already tending what came up in the clearing — deciding, pruning, handing things on — and you'd call it just getting by.
cells.ask: say out loud that one thing you've kept alive through this was your doing — the credit is yours, and taking it is what lets you release what's finished.
cells.core:
Tending that knows itself is simple and strong: you choose what to carry forward, you let what's done be done, and you can see your own hand in the shape things take. People get handed something real when they get handed something from you, and you know it as yours.

That's what's running here now. You're in the clearing every day — choosing, cutting back, passing things on — and the work is real. Yet you describe it like it's the shape things took, like it happened around you. It didn't. It's your hands. One thing you've kept alive through this. One thing you decided to carry. Say so, out loud. Release comes easier once you've taken the credit for finishing.
cells.sheetLine: The tending is already yours — taking the credit is what lets you let go.
